visualOpportunities.description: Over-shoulder person at a framed mirror; two reflected eyes and gaze targets. Push toward eyes while subjective state is clearly labeled. No third-person view falsely frozen. Camera icon beside same mirror portrait, then visibly transition to later playback with a moving iris. Recorded external view, not direct mirror perception. Pull back to shoulder and reflection, highlight that reflected eyes and observer are the same person. Optical link stays continuous. Same eye pivots in simplified side section; light from a fixed mirror feature falls on changing retinal positions. Not a detailed neural circuit. Carry eye and retinal sweep into a softly attenuated feature illustration; qualitative dip spans before/during/after, never a flat zero or blackout. Same eye closeup expands into before/blur/after sequence, then clear flank views visually dominate. Label perception schematic, time expanded. First-person mirror view shifts gaze target and resolves without black frames; stable perception illustration, not literal subjective recording or complete explanation of spatial constancy. Large camera/playback frame shows filmed iris moving while a small stationary viewer-eye motif establishes steady current gaze. Replay timeline distinct from original recording. Return to original person/mirror with continuous reflected movement on external view; momentary direct-perception annotation and confident resolved ending.

segments.text: Look from one eye to the other in a mirror. Why can't you normally catch the movement?
Now record your eyes, and watch it back. There it is.
Each quick jump is a saccade.
In the mirror, the eyes you're watching are also the eyes doing the looking.
As they turn, the image sweeps across the retina.
Visual sensitivity drops around the movement. That's saccadic suppression.
The clear views before and after can also mask the brief blur.
You aren't completely blind. These effects help keep vision stable.
Watching a recording later separates the movement from your own eye turn.
The mirror never stopped showing it. Your visual system normally keeps the sweep out of awareness.

misconceptionSafeguards: Normally and rapid movements, not universal impossibility.
No optical interruption of mirror reflection, no frozen physical iris.
Suppression stimulus selective and partial; masking a second contributor.
Retinal sweep and spatial displacement distinct; stable vision not explained by suppression alone.
First-person illustration labeled; no black frame, missing time or discrete literal brain snapshots.
Recorded camera playback later, steady current gaze; no equivalence to direct mirror perception.
Slowed motion and qualitative sensitivity curve labeled, no numerical measurement implied.
review.comprehensionReview: Demonstration precedes terminology. One portrait connects all views. Retinal sweep, sensitivity dip and masking get separate concrete moments; final playback makes timing the payoff.
review.rightsReview: All original code artwork and synthesized sound; existing licensed fonts and existing Apache2 local Kokoro. Sources research-only; no reproduced scientific figures or third-party imagery.

careAssessment.rationale: General nonclinical perception explanation; no diagnosis, treatment, eye manipulation or bright-light experiments.
